title: Windows, locks or radio stopped working
h1: Why did my power windows, locks or radio stop working?
metaDesc: Power windows, door locks or radio stopped working? Find out if it's a fuse, switch, motor, wiring or charging problem, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: window makes noise but wont move
intro: When windows, locks or the radio quit, the cause is usually local: a fuse, a switch, a motor or a wire. But if several things fail at once or other warning signs appear, it can point to a charging or wiring problem that matters more. A few questions will sort out which.
safety: If you smell burning plastic or see smoke from a door, the dash or under the hood, turn off the car, get out and keep away from it.
If a fuse blows again right after you replace it, stop replacing it. There's a short circuit that needs to be found.
Never replace a fuse with a higher-rated one. That can let wiring overheat and start a fire.

q_warning_signs.q: Did it happen along with any of these?

opts.a: A burning smell, smoke, or a switch or panel that feels hot
The battery light came on, or the lights and gauges are dimming or flickering
Right after rain, a car wash, an open window or water getting inside
None of these
I'm not sure
One or more power windows
Door locks or the key fob
The radio or center screen
Several different things at once (for example radio, power outlets and windows)
Things cut in and out, especially over bumps or when a door moves
I'm not sure

q_window.q: When you press the switch for the problem window, what happens?

opts.a: I hear a motor whir or grinding, but the glass doesn't move, or it dropped or tilted
None of the passenger windows work from their own switches, but they work from the driver's door
Nothing happens, and it's just one window
It moves very slowly or stops partway
I'm not sure
One door won't lock or unlock, and may buzz or click
The key fob doesn't work, but the lock switch inside the car does
No door responds to the inside switch or the fob
I'm not sure

q_radio.q: What is the radio or screen doing?

opts.a: It's asking for a code, or shows 'CODE' or 'LOCKED', after battery work or a jump
It's completely dead and dark
It turns on but freezes, restarts by itself or has no sound
I'm not sure

result.title: An electrical part or wire may be overheating. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: Turn the car off, take the key out and get everyone out. Don't use it again until it's inspected. Have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you see flames or heavy smoke, move well away and call 911.
If the smell came from one window switch or door, mention that to the shop. Some switches have been recalled for overheating, so check for recalls with your VIN.
result.why: A burning smell or a hot switch along with failed accessories means current is going where it shouldn't, and wiring is heating up. That can turn into a fire, so the car shouldn't be used until the cause is found.

causes.name: Shorted or water-damaged switch
causes.clues: The smell or heat is at one switch, often a window switch.

causes.name: Damaged or pinched wiring
causes.clues: Recent work behind a panel, or an aftermarket accessory was added.

causes.name: Overheated motor or connector
causes.clues: A window or seat motor that strained or stuck just before the smell.

you: Ask a dealer for your brand whether a recall affecting the electrical system is open on your VIN.
shop: Wiring and connector inspection for heat damage

result.title: The charging system may be failing, and accessories may be shutting down to save power
result.now: Get off the road somewhere safe and turn off electrical extras. Don't set out again until the battery and alternator have been tested. A mobile mechanic or a tow is the safest way to get it checked, because the car may shut off without much warning.
if: If the lights keep dimming, the steering gets heavy or the engine starts to stumble, get off the road right away. The car may shut off.
If the problem cleared after a jump start or new battery, still have the alternator tested.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the hood, turn the car off and get everyone out.
result.why: When voltage drops, many cars shut off non-essential accessories first, so windows and the radio can stop working before the engine does. A battery light suggests the car isn't charging properly, and a shop will usually test the battery, alternator and cables before replacing anything.

causes.name: Failing alternator
causes.clues: A battery light, a whining noise, or lights that dim at idle.

causes.name: Weak or failing battery
causes.clues: Slow cranking, or the battery is more than 4–5 years old.

causes.name: Loose or corroded battery or ground cable
causes.clues: Crusty terminals, or things flicker over bumps.

you: Check that the battery clamps are tight and clean.

result.title: Water may have gotten into a switch, connector or module
result.now: Dry the interior as much as you can, leave the affected switches alone for now, and have the electrical system checked within a few days.
if: If anything smells hot or burnt, turn the car off and don't use it until it's inspected.
If the carpet is wet, find where the water is getting in. Modules under the seats and carpet are easily damaged.
If the airbag light comes on, or the car won't start or acts on its own, have it checked before relying on it. Modules under the seats and carpet include safety systems on many cars.
result.why: Switches, connectors and control modules don't tolerate water. Moisture can make them stop working, act on their own, or short out. Some recover once dry; others are damaged. A shop will usually dry and test the connector or module before deciding whether anything needs replacing.

causes.name: Water in a door switch or connector
causes.clues: A window left open in rain, or problems on one door only.

causes.name: Wet control module
causes.clues: Damp carpet, or several unrelated things acting up.

causes.name: Blocked drains or leaking seals letting water in
causes.clues: Repeated wet carpet or a musty smell.

you: Check the carpet and under the floor mats for dampness.
Note which door or area got wet.
shop: Connector and module inspection for corrosion

result.title: A blown fuse is a common and easy thing to check first
result.now: Use your owner's manual to find the fuse for the item that stopped working, and replace it with one of the same rating if it's blown.
if: If the new fuse blows right away or soon after, stop replacing it. There's a short circuit, so book a repair.
If the fuses are fine and several things are still dead, have the wiring and control modules checked.
If you smell burning or see smoke, turn the car off and get out. Don't keep swapping fuses.
If what stopped working is something you need to drive safely, like headlights, wipers, brake lights or turn signals, get it fixed before driving in conditions where you need it.
result.why: Fuses protect circuits by burning out when something draws too much current. When several things on one circuit stop together, or something dies with no warning, a fuse is a quick first thing to check. A fuse that blows is a symptom, so if it keeps happening the shop will look for the short behind it.

causes.name: Blown fuse
causes.clues: Several things on the same circuit died at once, often after plugging something into a power outlet.

causes.name: Failed relay
causes.clues: The fuse is fine but nothing on that circuit works.

causes.name: Wiring or control module fault
causes.clues: Fuses are fine and other unrelated things act strangely.

you: Check the fuses in the interior and under-hood fuse boxes. A blown fuse has a broken metal strip inside.
Unplug any chargers or accessories from the power outlets.
shop: Short-circuit diagnosis if the fuse keeps blowing

result.title: The window regulator, the track that moves the glass, may have broken
result.now: Stop pressing the switch so the motor doesn't burn out, and book a repair. If the window is down, cover the opening to keep rain out.
if: If the glass has fallen into the door and the car must be left parked, secure the opening with plastic and tape and park somewhere protected.
If you smell burning from the door, stop using the switch and get it checked soon.
result.why: The motor is working if you hear it, but the regulator that carries the glass has broken a cable or a plastic clip. The glass then slips, tilts or drops into the door.

causes.name: Broken window regulator cable or clip
causes.clues: A snap or crunch, then the glass dropped or tilted.

causes.name: Stripped motor gear
causes.clues: The motor whirs freely but nothing moves at all.

causes.name: Glass came loose from its mount
causes.clues: The glass rattles or sits crooked in the frame.

you: Listen at the door while someone presses the switch.
shop: Door panel removal and regulator inspection

result.title: The window lock button on the driver's door may be turned on
result.now: Find the window lock button on the driver's door switch panel (often marked with a window and a lock or an X) and press it to turn it off.
if: If the passenger switches still don't work with the lock off, the master switch or wiring may be faulty. Book a check.
If just one passenger switch doesn't work, that switch is the likely problem.
result.why: The window lock disables the passenger window switches, usually so children can't open them. It's easy to bump by accident, and it makes the windows seem broken.

causes.name: Window lock button turned on
causes.clues: All passenger switches stopped together, but the driver can still move every window.

causes.name: Faulty driver's master switch
causes.clues: The lock button doesn't change anything.

causes.name: Wiring fault in the driver's door
causes.clues: Other driver's door functions act up too.

you: Press the window lock button and try the passenger switches again.

result.title: Possibly a worn window motor, switch or door wiring
result.now: Try the window from the driver's master switch as well as its own switch, then book a repair when convenient.
if: If it works from the driver's switch but not its own, that door's switch is a likely suspect.
If the window is stuck open, cover it and get it fixed soon to keep rain and thieves out.
If it moves slowly or stops partway, a dry or dirty window track or a tired motor are possibilities.
result.why: When a single window does nothing or struggles, the fault is usually in that door: its switch, its motor, or the wires that pass through the door hinge area, which flex every time the door opens.

causes.name: Worn window motor
causes.clues: It has been slow for a while, or it works if you tap the door panel.

causes.name: Faulty window switch
causes.clues: It works from the driver's master switch but not its own.

causes.name: Broken wire between the door and the body
causes.clues: Other things in that door (lock, mirror, speaker) also stopped.

you: Check whether the lock and speaker in that door still work.

result.title: The lock motor (actuator) in that door may be failing
result.now: Use the key or the manual lock on that door for now, and book a repair when convenient.
if: If the door won't open from inside or outside, get it fixed soon. It can be a problem in an emergency.
If other things in that door have also stopped, a broken wire in the door hinge area is more likely.
result.why: Each door has a small motor that moves the lock. They wear out over time, and a weak one often buzzes or clicks without moving the lock, especially in cold weather.

causes.name: Worn door lock actuator
causes.clues: A buzz or weak click from that door, or it works sometimes.

causes.name: Broken wire in the door hinge area
causes.clues: The window or mirror on that door also acts up.

causes.name: Frozen or sticky lock mechanism
causes.clues: It only happens in cold weather.

you: Listen at the door while someone presses the lock button.
Check whether other features in that door work.

result.title: A weak key fob battery is a common cause
result.now: Replace the key fob battery, which is usually a coin-type battery listed in your owner's manual.
if: If your spare fob works, the main fob's battery or the fob itself is the problem.
If neither fob works with new batteries, the car's receiver or the fobs may need checking or reprogramming by a dealer or locksmith.
result.why: If the switch inside the car locks and unlocks all the doors, the lock motors and wiring are working. That leaves the fob or the car's receiver, and a weak fob battery is a common cause and the easiest to try first.

causes.name: Dead fob battery
causes.clues: The range has been getting shorter.

causes.name: Damaged fob
causes.clues: It was dropped or got wet.

causes.name: Fob lost its programming or receiver fault
causes.clues: Neither fob works, even with new batteries.

result.title: The radio's anti-theft code needs to be entered
result.now: Look for the radio code card in your owner's manual or glove box and enter the code as the manual describes.
if: If you can't find the code, a dealer for your car's brand can usually look it up with your VIN and proof of ownership.
If you enter the wrong code several times, it may lock you out for a while. Leave the radio on and wait as the manual describes.
result.why: Many radios lock themselves when the battery is disconnected, as a theft deterrent. They need the original code before they'll work again. Usually nothing is broken.

causes.name: Anti-theft lock after the battery was disconnected or went flat
causes.clues: It started right after battery work or a dead battery.

causes.name: Radio needs to be re-paired with the car
causes.clues: A code doesn't work, or a message asks for a dealer.

you: Check the owner's manual for the code entry steps.

result.title: The radio or screen may need a software reset or update
result.now: Try a reset: turn the car off, open and close the driver's door, wait a few minutes, then restart. Check your owner's manual for a specific reset procedure.
if: If the screen also controls things like climate, defrost or the backup camera and those stop working, get it checked within a few days, and don't rely on the camera when reversing.
If it started after a phone was connected, try deleting the phone from the system and re-pairing it.
result.why: Modern radios are small computers. Freezing, rebooting or losing sound is often a software glitch that a reset or update fixes. If it keeps happening, the unit, its amplifier or its wiring may need repair.

causes.name: Software glitch
causes.clues: It comes and goes, and a restart temporarily fixes it.

causes.name: Failed amplifier or speaker wiring
causes.clues: The screen works but there's no sound from any speaker.

causes.name: Low battery voltage
causes.clues: It reboots when you start the car or use other accessories.

you: Note the software version shown in the infotainment settings, if available, and ask the shop whether an update applies.

result.title: A broken or loose wire is possible, often where the wires pass into a door
result.now: Note exactly what cuts out and when, then book an electrical diagnosis when convenient.
if: If you smell burning or anything feels hot, turn off the car and don't use it until it's inspected.
If the problems happen when the door opens or closes, the wires in the door hinge area are a likely place to check first.
If headlights, wipers or other lights cut out, don't drive at night or in bad weather until it's fixed.
result.why: Things that cut in and out with bumps or door movement usually come from a wire that's cracked inside its insulation, or a connector that's loose or corroded. The wires that run through the door hinge area flex constantly and are a common failure point.

causes.name: Broken wires in the door hinge boot
causes.clues: Problems with one door's windows, locks, mirror or speaker together.

causes.name: Loose or corroded ground connection
causes.clues: Several unrelated things flicker or reset over bumps.

causes.name: Loose connector behind a panel
causes.clues: It started after a stereo, alarm or other accessory was installed.

you: Open and close the door slowly while someone watches whether the feature cuts in and out.
